body:
Plain-language answer: we are ready to start building the movie foundation carefully, but we do not yet have a working end-to-end movie system.

What works today is the text-story system and much of the reusable machinery around it: narrative graphs, hierarchy, evidence/provenance, feature tracks, candidate proposals, deterministic resolution, recall-alignment structures, and renderer-neutral output. We also now have a reviewed movie architecture, time/evidence rules, a component-admission ledger, and an independently reviewed specification for the synthetic test movies.

What does not work yet: storymodel4s cannot ingest a movie into a checked media atlas; there is no landed movie clock/evidence API, FFmpeg reader, frame handoff, shot detector runtime, timed-dialogue lattice, speaker/face/character resolver, audiovisual feature pipeline, or movie-to-recall run. No source film has passed through the proposed contracts. So the honest answer to “does the movie system work?” is no—not yet. We are closer to a build-ready specification than to a finished product.

We need three different kinds of test material because no one dataset can prove everything:

1. A tiny project-authored synthetic movie family. This tests timestamps, gaps, variable frame timing, audio versus silence, timed text, pixel handoff, failures, replay, and shot-proposal plumbing. Its exact V3 specification has now passed two independent reviews. It proves engineering mechanics, not story understanding.
2. A lawful, exact open film excerpt. Big Buck Bunny remains the leading first candidate. It tests real container/codec and visual behavior, but it has no paired human recall and is not enough for the scientific goal.
3. An exact film edition paired with real human recalls. This is required to show that audiovisual source modeling actually improves recall alignment over transcript-only, visual-only, and audio-only baselines.

Sherlock is scientifically valuable and already connected to useful recall/neural work, but the exact episode bytes and linked annotation/workbook rights are unresolved. We should use it only if written artifact-level permission is obtained. It is not logically mandatory: an explicitly ratified replacement can take its place.

FilmFestival is probably the better first scientific scale because it has ten short films and recalls, but the public deposit omits the film files for copyright. We need the exact viewed editions plus participant/REB authority before it becomes a valid source-plus-recall benchmark. Public recall files alone are not enough.

If Sherlock and FilmFestival remain blocked, the clean alternative is to create or obtain an open short-film/staged-event corpus prospectively: exact lawful stimuli first, then consented recalls under a recorded protocol. That may ultimately be more reproducible than reverse-engineering uncertain legacy rights.

The remaining order is: close the real-transcript research gate and source/rights gate; land the final time-contract amendment; implement the portable media clocks/evidence types; build and test the synthetic fixtures; admit one open film; then run an exact paired recall study. Speech, identity, visual/audio models, and omni-models come after those foundations and each must earn admission separately.

Bottom line: the conceptual risk is substantially reduced; the implementation and empirical proof are still ahead. We need test corpora, but we need exact lawful editions and declared scientific roles—not a pile of loosely related downloads.
